title: opRevolve Symmetric Body
summary: Revolve a 2D profile around an axis to create any rotationally symmetric solid: cones, domes, vases, spools, pulleys, or tapered rods. The profile must be a closed region with the axis line on one edge.
parameterHints: Expose all radii and heights as isLength parameters.
If the shape tapers, expose both base radius and top radius separately.
Use isLength(definition.topRadius, NONNEGATIVE_ZERO_INCLUSIVE_LENGTH_BOUNDS) so top radius can legally be 0 (sharp tip).
modelingNotes: The sketch must contain the axis line as one segment (on x=0 or along y=0) AND the profile outline as connected segments or spline on the other side.
skSolve the sketch BEFORE calling opRevolve.
The revolve axis in FeatureScript is a Line value: line(skPlane.origin, skPlane.normal). Never pass a Query as the axis.
Full revolution: angleForward = 2 * PI * radian. Half section: PI * radian.
The profile and axis must form a closed region — connect top, side, and bottom segments.
featurePattern: sketch axis line + profile segments/spline on one side, skSolve, opRevolve with line() axis and 2*PI*radian angleForward.
failureModes: Passing qSketchRegion or qCreatedBy as the revolve axis — axis must be a Line value.
Forgetting to close the profile — an open profile produces no solid region.
Using definition.radius * inch when radius is already a Length from isLength — this doubles units.
A 2-point skFitSpline is too simple; use at least 4 control points for organic curves.
validationRules: Profile must stay on one side of the axis (all x >= 0 if axis is vertical).
Top and bottom of profile must connect to the axis.
example_prompt: Cone 2 inch base radius, 3 inch tall, sharp tip

title: opLoft Between Two Profiles
summary: opLoft transitions a solid between two or more cross-section sketches on separate planes. Use for tapered boxes, airfoils, transition fittings, and any shape where the cross-section changes along its length.
parameterHints: Each profile sketch must be on a separate plane.
Create the second plane with: plane(skPlane.origin + skPlane.normal * definition.height, skPlane.normal).
Expose the height between profiles and any radius or dimension change.
modelingNotes: opLoft takes an 'edges' array of qSketchRegion queries — one per profile — in order from start to end.
opLoft NEVER takes a 'sections' key. Only 'edges' and 'vertices'.
Both profiles must be solved (skSolve) before calling opLoft.
For a tapered cylinder: profile 1 = large circle, profile 2 = smaller circle on offset plane.
For a tapered box: profile 1 = wide rectangle, profile 2 = narrower rectangle.
The profiles do not need to be the same shape — a circle can loft to a square.
Use more than 2 profiles for S-curve or waisted shapes.
featurePattern: sketchA on planeA (large profile) + sketchB on planeB (small profile), both skSolve'd, then opLoft edges:[qSketchRegion(id+'skA'), qSketchRegion(id+'skB')].
failureModes: Adding 'sections' key to opLoft — that key does not exist in FS.
Passing the sketch variable instead of the id string to qSketchRegion.
Profiles that are too different in shape can produce twisted loft geometry — use guide curves if needed.
Both profiles must be separate sketches — you cannot loft within a single sketch.
validationRules: At least 2 profile entries required in the edges array.
All profile sketches must be solved before opLoft.
example_prompt: Transition fitting from 2 inch square to 1 inch circle, 3 inches tall

title: opSweep Profile Along Path
summary: Sweep a cross-section profile along a path curve to create pipes, bent tubes, curved handles, hooks, and rails. The profile sketch is on a plane perpendicular to the path start.
parameterHints: Expose the profile radius or dimensions and the path geometry dimensions separately.
For a circular tube, profile is a circle with the tube's outer radius.
For a hollow tube, profile is two concentric circles.
modelingNotes: opSweep takes 'profiles' (qSketchRegion of the cross-section) and 'path' (qCreatedBy of the path sketch edges).
The path sketch must produce wire edges — use skLineSegment, skArc, or skFitSpline.
The profile plane should be perpendicular to the path at its start point.
For a simple L-shaped path: sketch two connected skLineSegments in an L, solve, then sweep a circle profile.
For a curved path: use skArc or skFitSpline in the path sketch.
Path edges are queried with qCreatedBy(id + 'pathSk', EntityType.EDGE), not qSketchRegion.
featurePattern: pathSketch (open wire curve) + profileSketch (closed cross-section on perpendicular plane), both skSolve'd, opSweep profiles:qSketchRegion(profile) path:qCreatedBy(pathId, EntityType.EDGE).
failureModes: Using qSketchRegion for the path — path must use qCreatedBy with EntityType.EDGE.
Profile plane not perpendicular to path start — causes twisted geometry.
An open profile cross-section produces a sheet, not a solid.
Path sketch must be wire (open or closed curve) — not a region.
validationRules: Profile must be a closed region sketch.
Path must be a connected edge wire — not a region.
example_prompt: Bent pipe 0.5 inch outer diameter following a 90 degree arc of 3 inch radius

title: opShell Hollow Body
summary: opShell hollows out a solid body to a specified wall thickness, optionally leaving one or more faces open. Use for enclosures, boxes, cups, and shells.
parameterHints: Expose wallThickness as an isLength parameter.
If a face is left open, expose a boolean toggle like 'Open Top'.
Wall thickness for plastic: 0.04 to 0.15 inch. For sheet metal: 0.03 to 0.125 inch.
modelingNotes: opShell must be called AFTER the solid body is created (after opExtrude or opRevolve).
The 'entities' field takes the solid body query: qCreatedBy(id + 'ext1', EntityType.BODY).
The 'excludeFaces' field removes those faces from the shelling operation — they become open holes.
Use qCapEntity(id + 'ext1', CapType.START) to open the bottom face.
Use qCapEntity(id + 'ext1', CapType.END) to open the top face.
opShell on a complex body can fail — prefer sketching the hollow profile directly for simple shapes.
featurePattern: opExtrude solid box, then opShell with thickness and excludeFaces to open top or bottom.
failureModes: Calling opShell before the solid body exists — must extrude first.
Wall thickness larger than half the smallest dimension causes opShell to fail.
opShell often fails on bodies with fillets or complex topology — apply shell before fillets.
validationRules: wallThickness must be less than half the smallest dimension.
Apply shell before opFillet for best results.
example_prompt: Open-top rectangular box 4x3x2 inches with 0.1 inch walls

title: opFillet Rounded Edges
summary: opFillet rounds selected edges. Use to soften corners on mechanical parts, reduce stress concentrations, and add visual polish.
parameterHints: Expose filletRadius as an isLength parameter with NONNEGATIVE_ZERO_INCLUSIVE_LENGTH_BOUNDS.
Check filletRadius > 0 before calling opFillet to avoid an error with zero radius.
Maximum fillet radius is limited by adjacent face size — typically less than half the narrowest face width.
modelingNotes: opFillet entities field: qEdgeTopologyFilter(qOwnedByBody(qCreatedBy(id+'ext1', EntityType.BODY), EntityType.EDGE), EdgeTopology.TWO_SIDED) selects all convex edges.
To fillet only top edges: filter by position after evaluateQuery.
Apply opFillet AFTER all boolean operations — filleting before subtraction causes failures.
Only fillet edges that actually exist on the body — querying non-existent edges throws an error.
Separate fillet operations with different radii on different edge sets.
featurePattern: opExtrude body, then if filletRadius > 0*inch: opFillet with qEdgeTopologyFilter selecting TWO_SIDED edges on the body.
failureModes: Fillet radius larger than adjacent face — geometry becomes invalid.
Filleting before boolean subtract — causes topology conflicts.
qEdgeTopologyFilter must use TWO_SIDED for convex edges, ONE_SIDED for boundary edges.
example_prompt: Box with 0.25 inch fillets on all edges

title: opChamfer Beveled Edges
summary: opChamfer bevels selected edges at a 45-degree angle. Use on mating faces, sharp corners, and thread chamfers.
parameterHints: Use ChamferType.EQUAL_OFFSETS for a symmetric 45-degree chamfer.
Use ChamferType.OFFSET_ANGLE for a specified angle.
Typical chamfer width: 0.02 to 0.1 inch.
modelingNotes: opChamfer syntax: { 'entities': edgeQuery, 'chamferType': ChamferType.EQUAL_OFFSETS, 'width': definition.chamferWidth }
For OFFSET_ANGLE: { 'chamferType': ChamferType.OFFSET_ANGLE, 'width': ..., 'angle': 45 * degree }
Apply after all boolean operations, same as opFillet.
Typically used on leading edges of bolts, shafts, and thread starts.
featurePattern: opExtrude body, then opChamfer with ChamferType.EQUAL_OFFSETS and width parameter on selected edges.
failureModes: Chamfer width larger than adjacent face — invalid geometry.
Wrong ChamferType enum name — use ChamferType.EQUAL_OFFSETS, not ChamferType.SYMMETRIC.
validationRules: chamferWidth must be smaller than shortest adjacent edge.
example_prompt: Cylinder with 0.05 inch chamfer on the top rim

title: Circular Pattern With opPattern
summary: Repeat geometry around a central axis using opPattern with PatternType.CIRCULAR. Use for bolt hole patterns, fin arrays, spokes, and radial features.
parameterHints: Expose instanceCount as isInteger and the circle axis (or use the sketch plane normal).
For bolt holes: instanceCount and boltCircleRadius are the main params.
PatternType.CIRCULAR requires: axis (Line), instanceCount, angle (total sweep, usually 2*PI*radian for full circle).
modelingNotes: opPattern creates copies of a body or feature.
For circular body patterns: { 'entities': qCreatedBy(id+'feat1', EntityType.BODY), 'patternType': PatternType.CIRCULAR, 'axis': line(origin, normal), 'instanceCount': N, 'angle': 2*PI*radian }
Alternatively, use a for loop in the sketch to place all circles at once — simpler and more reliable.
For-loop approach: for (var k = 0; k < N; k += 1) { var a = 2*PI*k/N; skCircle(sk, 'hole'~k, { 'center': vector(boltR*cos(a), boltR*sin(a))*inch, 'radius': holeR }); }
The for-loop sketch approach is preferred for holes because all holes are in a single sketch and extrude together.
featurePattern: For hole patterns: for loop in sketch placing circles at angle = 2*PI*k/N around bolt circle radius. For solid feature copies: opPattern with PatternType.CIRCULAR.
failureModes: Using opPattern on a body before boolean — results in overlapping bodies.
Forgetting to union patterned bodies — leaves them as separate solids.
for-loop sketch approach is simpler and more reliable than opPattern for holes.
example_prompt: 6 bolt holes on a 3 inch bolt circle

title: Linear Pattern Array
summary: Repeat a feature or body at equal spacing along an axis using opPattern with PatternType.LINEAR or a for loop in a sketch.
parameterHints: Expose instanceCount and spacing as editable parameters.
Total span = spacing * (instanceCount - 1).
modelingNotes: For a linear array of holes or slots in a sketch: use a for loop placing rectangles or circles at x offsets.
For-loop sketch: for (var i = 0; i < N; i += 1) { var cx = startX + i * spacing; skCircle(sk, 'h'~i, {...}); }
For opPattern solid copy: { 'patternType': PatternType.LINEAR, 'entities': bodyQuery, 'direction': skPlane.x, 'distance': spacing, 'instanceCount': N }
opPattern LINEAR needs a direction vector (skPlane.x, skPlane.y, or skPlane.normal).
featurePattern: For holes/slots: for loop in sketch with x offset. For solid features: opPattern LINEAR with direction, distance, instanceCount.
failureModes: Pattern direction must be a unit vector — use skPlane.x, skPlane.y, or skPlane.normal.
For-loop variable names must be unique strings per iteration: 'hole' ~ k is correct.
validationRules: Total span must fit within the body.
example_prompt: 4 evenly spaced holes along a plate

title: Boolean Subtract Cut
summary: Use opBoolean with BooleanOperationType.SUBTRACTION to cut holes, pockets, and slots by subtracting a tool body from a target. Required for any internal cavity that cannot be sketched directly.
parameterHints: The tool body is what gets cut away. The target body is what remains.
Build the tool body first (smaller shape), then subtract from the larger target.
modelingNotes: opBoolean subtract: { 'tools': qCreatedBy(id+'tool', EntityType.BODY), 'targets': qCreatedBy(id+'main', EntityType.BODY), 'operationType': BooleanOperationType.SUBTRACTION }
The tool body is consumed by the subtraction — it no longer exists as a separate body after.
For cylindrical holes: sketch a circle + extrude beyond the body + subtract.
Simpler: use a sketch with the hole profile in the same sketch as the outer profile and extrude with qSketchRegion(id, true) — this auto-subtracts inner regions.
qSketchRegion(id + 'sk1', true) means 'use all regions, treating inner ones as cuts' — prefer this over boolean for simple cases.
featurePattern: Build tool cylinder (opExtrude or opCylinder), then opBoolean SUBTRACTION with tools=toolBody targets=mainBody.
failureModes: Tool body not fully overlapping the target — the cut will be shallow or miss entirely.
Wrong operationType enum — must be BooleanOperationType.SUBTRACTION.
Tool body must be separate from target body — cannot subtract from itself.
validationRules: Prefer qSketchRegion(id, true) for holes in the same sketch over boolean subtract.
example_prompt: Box with a cylindrical pocket cut in the top face

title: Cone Or Tapered Frustum
summary: Model cones, truncated cones, funnels, nozzles, and tapered rods by revolving a closed trapezoidal profile around the vertical axis. Set top radius to 0 for a sharp tip.
parameterHints: Expose bottomRadius, topRadius (0 for sharp tip), and height.
Use NONNEGATIVE_ZERO_INCLUSIVE_LENGTH_BOUNDS for topRadius so 0 is allowed.
For a funnel: large topRadius, small bottomRadius.
modelingNotes: Sketch a closed trapezoid: axis line on x=0, then base at y=0, slanted side, top at y=height, and close back to axis.
Revolve with line(skPlane.origin, skPlane.normal) as axis and 2*PI*radian.
bRv = definition.bottomRadius / inch; tRv = definition.topRadius / inch; htv = definition.height / inch.
Segments: axis(0,0)→(0,htv), base(0,0)→(bRv,0), side(bRv,0)→(tRv,htv), top(tRv,htv)→(0,htv).
For a carrot: use a revolved spline with 5 control points that taper and slightly curve inward near the tip.
featurePattern: Closed trapezoidal profile (axis + base + slanted side + top cap), skSolve, opRevolve with line() axis.
failureModes: Open profile — all 4 segments must connect to form a closed region.
topRadius equal to or greater than bottomRadius for a normal cone — check relationship.
If topRadius = 0 exactly, the tip vertex must exactly touch the axis.
validationRules: topRadius >= 0 and topRadius < bottomRadius for a standard cone.
example_prompt: Cone 1.5 inch base, 4 inches tall, sharp tip

title: Organic Carrot Or Root Shape
summary: Organic tapered shapes like carrots and roots use a revolved spline profile. The spline side has 5+ control points curving inward from base to tip. The profile is closed with an axis line and base segment.
parameterHints: Expose baseRadius (widest point, at y=0) and height (total length).
The tip is always at (x=0, y=height) — touching the axis.
Control points at 20%, 45%, 70%, 85%, and 100% of height with decreasing radius.
modelingNotes: Spline control points (bRv = baseRadius/inch, htv = height/inch):
vector(bRv, 0)*inch, vector(bRv*0.9, htv*0.2)*inch, vector(bRv*0.7, htv*0.45)*inch, vector(bRv*0.4, htv*0.7)*inch, vector(0.02, htv)*inch
Close the profile: skLineSegment 'top' from (0.02,htv) to (0,htv), skLineSegment 'axis' from (0,0) to (0,htv), skLineSegment 'base' from (0,0) to (bRv,0).
skFitSpline 'profile' with these 5 points on the right side.
Revolve with line(skPlane.origin, skPlane.normal) and 2*PI*radian.
The 5-point spline gives the characteristic gentle taper of an organic root — 2 points produces a straight line (cone), not organic.
featurePattern: axis + base + 5-point skFitSpline + top connector segments forming closed region, revolve 360°.
failureModes: Spline with only 2 points is a straight line — not organic.
Spline control points must be on one side of the axis (x > 0) — negative x causes a self-intersecting profile.
Profile must close: tip of spline must connect back to axis via a short line.
validationRules: Last spline point must be close to x=0 to join the axis.
example_prompt: Parametric carrot shape 0.75 inch base diameter 4 inches long

title: Dome Or Hemisphere
summary: A dome or hemisphere is a revolved semicircle. Sketch a quarter-circle arc plus axis line, solve, then revolve 360 degrees.
parameterHints: Expose domeRadius as the main parameter.
For a flattened elliptical dome, expose domeRadius and domeHeight separately.
modelingNotes: Sketch: axis line from (0,0) to (0,R), arc from (R,0) to (0,R), base line from (0,0) to (R,0).
skArc: { 'start': vector(R,0)*inch, 'mid': vector(R*0.707, R*0.707)*inch, 'end': vector(0,R)*inch }
Revolve: line(skPlane.origin, skPlane.normal), 2*PI*radian.
For a full sphere: sketch a full semicircle (axis + right semicircle arc) and revolve.
For Hitch Peg head: build shaft with opCylinder first, then revolve dome centered at shaft top, then opBoolean UNION.
featurePattern: Quarter-circle arc + axis + base, skSolve, opRevolve 360° around plane normal.
failureModes: Arc mid-point must be at the 45-degree point: vector(R*cos(45°), R*sin(45°)) ≈ vector(0.707R, 0.707R).
Axis must be a Line value — not a query or variable reference.
Profile must be closed.
validationRules: Arc start must be on x-axis (y=0), arc end must be on y-axis (x=0).
Arc mid-point at 45 degrees: x and y both equal R * sqrt(2)/2.
example_prompt: Hemispherical dome 2 inch radius on a flat base

title: Pipe Along Arc Or L-Path
summary: An elbow pipe or bent tube is created by sweeping a circular cross-section along an arc or L-shaped path. The path sketch is wire edges; the profile sketch is a perpendicular circle.
parameterHints: Expose tubeRadius (profile circle radius) and bendRadius (arc radius of the path).
For 90-degree elbow: path arc from (0,0) sweeping 90° at bendRadius.
modelingNotes: Path sketch: draw an arc (skArc) on the sketch plane — this is the centerline of the pipe.
Profile sketch: draw a circle on a plane perpendicular to the path at its start point.
Perpendicular plane: plane(startPoint, pathTangent) where pathTangent is the direction of the path at its start.
For a simple L-path: two connected skLineSegments forming 90° corner, then sweep a circle along them.
opSweep: { 'profiles': qSketchRegion(id+'prof'), 'path': qCreatedBy(id+'path', EntityType.EDGE) }
Path edges are queried with EntityType.EDGE, not qSketchRegion.
featurePattern: Arc path sketch + perpendicular circle profile sketch, both skSolve'd, opSweep profiles=region path=edge.
failureModes: Using qSketchRegion for the path — path must be EntityType.EDGE.
Profile plane not perpendicular to path tangent — produces twisted tube.
Hollow pipe: use two concentric circles in the profile sketch and qSketchRegion(id, true).
validationRules: Profile must be a closed region.
example_prompt: 90 degree pipe elbow 0.5 inch radius tube on 2 inch bend radius

title: Box With Boss Or Raised Pad
summary: A boss is a raised cylindrical or rectangular platform on a flat surface. Build it by extruding the main box, then extruding a smaller boss profile from the top face using a second sketch and additive extrude.
parameterHints: Expose boxWidth, boxHeight, boxDepth for the base, and bossRadius and bossHeight for the raised feature.
Boss diameter is typically 1.5 to 2.5x the screw diameter it supports.
modelingNotes: Method 1 (simple): Create the base box with opExtrude. Then create a second sketch on the top face plane and extrude the boss geometry. Use opBoolean UNION to join the two bodies.

Method 2 (single sketch): Include both the outer rectangle and boss circle in one sketch only if no overlap — extrude both regions at the box height, then add-extrude the boss circle again for extra boss height.
Method 3 (additive extrude in FS): extrude the boss circle with 'operationType': NewBodyOperationType.ADD — this adds to the existing body without opBoolean.
For best results: separate extrudes + opBoolean UNION.
featurePattern: opExtrude base box, create offsetPlane at box top, newSketchOnPlane on offsetPlane, sketch boss circle, skSolve, opExtrude boss, opBoolean UNION.
failureModes: Boss extruded from world plane instead of offset plane at top of box — boss sinks into body.
Forgetting to union — leaves boss as separate body.
Boss radius must be smaller than box half-width.
validationRules: Boss plane = plane(boxOrigin + boxNormal * boxDepth, boxNormal).
example_prompt: 2x2x1 inch plate with a 0.25 inch radius boss 0.5 inch tall in the center

title: T-Bracket Or T-Plate
summary: A T-bracket is two rectangles forming a T cross-section extruded to length. Sketch the T profile as a closed polygon: the wide top flange plus the narrow vertical web.
parameterHints: Expose flangeWidth, flangeThickness, webHeight, webThickness, and length.
Typical structural T: flangeWidth = 2 * webHeight, flangeThickness = webThickness.
modelingNotes: Sketch the T profile as 8 connected line segments forming a closed T outline.
Center the flange on x=0. Web drops down from the center of the flange.
Points (flangeW=flangeWidth/inch, flangeT=flangeThickness/inch, webH=webHeight/inch, webT=webThickness/inch):
(-flangeW/2, 0) → (flangeW/2, 0) → (flangeW/2, flangeT) → (webT/2, flangeT) → (webT/2, flangeT+webH) → (-webT/2, flangeT+webH) → (-webT/2, flangeT) → (-flangeW/2, flangeT) → close.
Extrude along skPlane.normal (the length direction).
featurePattern: 8-segment closed T polygon (flange + web), skSolve, opExtrude to length.
failureModes: Open polygon — all 8 segments must connect back to start.
Web not centered on flange — check x-symmetry.
flangeThickness > 0 required — T profile has nonzero flange thickness.
validationRules: Profile must be closed — final segment returns to start point.
example_prompt: T-bracket 2 inch flange, 1 inch web, 0.125 inch wall, 6 inches long

title: U-Channel Or C-Channel
summary: A U-channel (or C-channel) is an open structural profile: flat web with two parallel flanges. Sketch as a closed U polygon and extrude to length. Do NOT use opShell — sketch the profile directly.
parameterHints: Expose channelWidth, channelHeight, wallThickness, and length.
FRC MAXTube: 2x1 inch cross-section, 0.1 inch wall.
For open channel: do NOT close the top. For box tube: add top wall to close it.
modelingNotes: U-channel profile: 6 segments. Bottom (web) goes full width. Two flanges go up from each end. Inner cavity is based on wall thickness.
Points (W=width/inch, H=height/inch, t=wall/inch):
This is an 8-segment closed U with inner cavity.
For box tube: add (0,H)→(W,H) closing segment becomes the top wall — use two nested rectangles instead.
Box tube: outer rectangle + inner rectangle (inset by wall), extrude the ring region.
featurePattern: 8-segment closed U polygon (outer U minus inner cavity), skSolve, opExtrude to channel length.
failureModes: Using opShell — fails on thin-walled shapes, prefer direct profile sketch.
Open profile — U must be closed for extrusion to work.
Wall thickness must be less than half width AND half height.
example_prompt: 2x1 inch aluminum U-channel 12 inches long 0.1 inch wall

title: Hex Nut Or Polygon Nut
summary: A hex nut is a regular hexagonal prism with a central threaded through-hole. Use skRegularPolygon for the hex outline and a concentric circle for the through-hole, then extrude the ring region.
parameterHints: acrossFlats is the standard dimension for nuts — convert: circumradius = acrossFlats / (sqrt(3)) for a hex.
Or: circumradius = acrossFlats / 2 / cos(30°) = acrossFlats * 0.5774.
Standard metric nuts: M4 AF=7mm, M5 AF=8mm, M6 AF=10mm, M8 AF=13mm.
Expose acrossFlats (or circumradius), throughHoleRadius, and thickness.
modelingNotes: Use skRegularPolygon for the hex — NOT skPolygon (it doesn't exist).
skRegularPolygon: { 'center': vector(0,0)*inch, 'firstVertex': vector(R,0)*inch, 'sides': 6 }
Also sketch a concentric circle for the through-hole.
Extrude with qSketchRegion(id, true) to get the ring region (hex minus hole).
For M6: AF=10mm=0.394in, circumradius=0.228in, throughHoleRadius=3mm=0.118in, thickness=5mm=0.197in.
featurePattern: skRegularPolygon (hex, sides=6) + inner circle, extrude with qSketchRegion(true).
failureModes: Using 'skPolygon' — it does not exist in FS. Always use skRegularPolygon.
acrossFlats is not the circumradius — circumradius = acrossFlats * 0.5774.
qSketchRegion without true parameter — extrudes solid hex including hole.
validationRules: sides must be 6 for a standard hex nut.
example_prompt: M8 hex nut (13mm across flats, 8mm thread)

title: Stepped Hollow Shaft Or Counterbore
summary: A shaft with multiple diameters and an axial bore. Combine two coaxial cylinders (or a sketch with step profile) and subtract a central bore. Common for motor output shafts, axles, and counterbored holes.
parameterHints: Expose mainRadius, stepRadius, boreRadius, mainLength, stepLength.
boreRadius < stepRadius always.
For counterbore: larger bore at top, smaller bore through bottom.
modelingNotes: Build stepped outer: two opCylinder calls + opBoolean UNION.
Then subtract bore: opCylinder for the bore tool, extend it beyond the full length, opBoolean SUBTRACTION.
Or: sketch the step profile as a revolve (two-step staircase shape) — faster and cleaner.
Revolve approach: axis on x=0, step profile with two widths, two heights, revolve 360°.
featurePattern: Revolve two-step staircase profile (4 horizontal + 4 vertical segments + axis) for clean stepped shaft with bore.
failureModes: boreRadius >= stepRadius causes empty body.
Bore not fully spanning the length — leaves closed-bottom counterbore instead of through-hole.
example_prompt: Stepped shaft 0.5 inch OD 1 inch long, 0.375 inch OD 0.75 inch long, 0.25 inch through bore

title: Rounded Rectangle Or Stadium Shape
summary: A rectangle with fully rounded ends (stadium shape) is used for slots, links, and structural caps. Sketch as a rectangle with two semicircles on the short ends, or as a slot profile.
parameterHints: Expose totalLength, width, and depth.
The semicircle radius = width / 2.
Center-to-center distance = totalLength - width.
modelingNotes: Sketch: two straight lines on top and bottom, two semicircular arcs on left and right ends.
Top line: from (-cc/2, R) to (cc/2, R). Bottom: same negated Y.
Left arc: skArc from (-cc/2, R) through (-cc/2 - R, 0) to (-cc/2, -R).
Right arc: skArc from (cc/2, -R) through (cc/2 + R, 0) to (cc/2, R).
where R = width/2/inch and cc = totalLength/inch - 2*R.
Alternatively: skRectangle + two skCircle at each end center, extrude all regions.
featurePattern: Two lines + two semicircle arcs forming closed stadium, skSolve, opExtrude to depth.
failureModes: Arc midpoints must be correct — at 90° from start/end points.
Arcs must connect exactly to the line endpoints.
example_prompt: Oblong slot 3 inches long 1 inch wide 0.25 inch thick

title: Cross Or Plus Shape
summary: A plus or cross shape is two overlapping rectangles. Use a single sketch with both rectangles — FS will naturally extrude their union as the cross region.
parameterHints: Expose armWidth (width of each arm) and totalSpan (tip to tip in one direction), and depth.
For a symmetric cross: both arms have the same armWidth and totalSpan.
modelingNotes: Sketch two centered rectangles in the same sketch:
Rectangle 1 (horizontal): -span/2 to +span/2 wide, -armW/2 to +armW/2 tall.
Rectangle 2 (vertical): -armW/2 to +armW/2 wide, -span/2 to +span/2 tall.
When both are in one sketch, FS extrudes their union as the cross profile.
Use skRectangle twice with different firstCorner/secondCorner values.
featurePattern: Two overlapping skRectangle calls in one sketch (horizontal arm + vertical arm), skSolve, opExtrude.
failureModes: Rectangles must overlap at the center — if they don't touch, two separate bodies are created.
Do not use two separate sketches and boolean union — one sketch is simpler and correct.
validationRules: Both rectangles must share the same center.
example_prompt: Cross bracket 4 inch span 0.5 inch arm width 0.25 inch thick

title: Torus Or Ring Solid
summary: A torus is created by revolving a circle offset from the axis. The circle center is at (R, 0) where R is the major radius, and the circle has minor radius r.
parameterHints: Expose majorRadius (center of tube to torus center) and minorRadius (tube radius).
majorRadius > minorRadius always.
For an O-ring: minorRadius is the cord diameter / 2.
modelingNotes: Sketch a circle centered at (majorRadius/inch, 0) with radius = minorRadius/inch.
The sketch plane normal is the revolution axis.
Revolve 360° around the vertical axis: line(skPlane.origin, skPlane.normal).
The circle must NOT intersect the revolution axis (majorRadius > minorRadius).
featurePattern: Off-axis circle at (R, 0), skSolve, opRevolve 360° around origin normal axis.
failureModes: Circle center on the axis (majorRadius=0) produces a sphere, not a torus.
Circle overlapping axis (majorRadius < minorRadius) — invalid geometry.
Revolution axis must pass through the sketch origin, not the circle center.
example_prompt: Torus with 2 inch major radius and 0.25 inch tube radius

title: Robot Mech Body Composition
summary: Robotic mech bodies are built from multiple rectangular extrusions (torso, head, limbs) assembled in one feature. Build each section as an opExtrude on a sketched region, then union adjacent sections.
parameterHints: Expose overall width, height, depth as fractions of the mech scale.
Each body part is a fraction of the main dimensions — torso is 40% of total height.
Default mech: width=12in, height=12in, depth=6in. Scale all parts proportionally.
modelingNotes: Build all mech parts in one sketch, one extrude, one feature:
Torso: rectangle centered at (0, body_y) with torso width and height.
Head: smaller rectangle centered at (0, head_y) above torso.
Left/Right arms: rectangles at (±arm_x, arm_y) beside torso.
Left/Right legs: rectangles at (±leg_x, leg_y) below torso.
Use skRectangle for each part in a single sketch.
All rectangles share one sketch → one extrude → all parts at same depth.
For varying depths, use multiple sketches and extrude + opBoolean UNION.
fsPoint helper: define a helper that builds a FS vector string for each corner.
featurePattern: Multiple skRectangle in one sketch (torso + head + arms + legs as separate non-overlapping rects), skSolve, opExtrude to body depth.
failureModes: Overlapping rectangles in the same sketch — FS auto-unions overlapping regions, which is fine for adjacent parts but can cause unexpected geometry for widely separated parts.
Parts too far apart — create disconnected bodies in the sketch region.
Too many sketch regions can slow sketch solving — keep under 20 rectangles.
validationRules: All part rectangles must be in pixel space relative to the mech center.
All extrude to same depth for a flat mech.
example_prompt: Blocky humanoid robot mech 12 inches tall with arms and legs

title: Propeller Or Fan Blade
summary: A simple fan blade is a twisted extruded airfoil. Approximate with a thin swept profile — a rectangle or lens shape swept along a radial line, with a twist applied by rotating the profile at the tip.
parameterHints: Expose bladeLength, bladeChord (width), bladeThickness, and pitchAngle.
For a simple prop: chord = 0.2 * bladeLength, thickness = 0.02 * bladeLength.
Hub radius is typically 0.15 * bladeLength.
modelingNotes: Simple approach: extrude a thin rectangle, then apply a twist — FS does not have native twist, so approximate.
Better approach: loft between two profile sketches — base chord aligned at 0°, tip chord rotated by pitchAngle.
Profile 1 at hub plane: horizontal rectangle (chord x thickness).
Profile 2 at tip plane (hub + bladeLength): same rectangle rotated by pitchAngle in its plane.
Use opLoft with 2 profiles for a twisted-looking blade.
Repeat for N blades using for loop with rotation: plane rotated around z-axis by 360/N degrees each iteration.
Full propeller: loft one blade, opPattern circular N blades around axis.
featurePattern: Loft between root profile and rotated tip profile for one blade, then opPattern circular for all blades.
failureModes: FS has no native twist operation — must use loft between rotated profiles.
opPattern must union blades to hub after patterning.
validationRules: Hub must be large enough to connect all blade roots.
example_prompt: 3-blade propeller 6 inch diameter 15 degree pitch

title: Spring Or Helix (Approximation)
summary: FeatureScript does not have a native helix sweep. Approximate a compression spring by stacking thin torus slices or using a multi-segment sweep path. For most uses, a simplified coil stack is sufficient.
parameterHints: Expose coilDiameter, wireDiameter, numberOfCoils, and freeLength.
Pitch = freeLength / numberOfCoils.
modelingNotes: FS does not support true helical sweep paths natively in custom features.
Approximation method: stack thin torus slices with vertical offset = pitch per coil, 12 slices per coil.
Each slice: off-axis circle at (coilR, 0), offset plane at y = slice_height, revolve 360°, union all.
Or: use Onshape's built-in Helix feature if available (not a FeatureScript call in custom features).
For decorative springs: stack 30° revolve segments with slight z-offset each.
Practical recommendation: note to user that a true spring helix requires the Onshape standard Helix feature.
featurePattern: Stack of thin-torus revolves at pitch intervals (approximation), or flag to user that Onshape's standard Helix feature is more appropriate.
failureModes: FS cannot produce a true helical geometry in a single opSweep — the path would need to be a 3D helix which requires a parametric path.
Too many union operations can slow regeneration.
example_prompt: Compression spring 1 inch coil diameter 0.1 inch wire diameter 6 coils 2 inch free length

title: Nozzle Or Spout Shape
summary: A nozzle combines a large input cone frustum and a small output cylindrical tip. Build as opLoft between a large circle and a small circle, or as a cone + cylinder union.
parameterHints: Expose inletRadius, outletRadius, coneTaper (the tapered section length), and outletLength.
For a rocket nozzle: convergent section + throat + divergent section.
modelingNotes: Simple nozzle: revolve a trapezoid (inlet face wide, outlet face narrow) + extend with a straight cylinder at the tip.
Profile: (0,0) axis, (inR,0) base, slant to (outR, taper), then (outR, taper+tipLen), back to (0, taper+tipLen).
Revolve 360° for the outer shell.
For a hollow nozzle with wall thickness: sketch both inner and outer profiles, revolve to get a hollow shell.
Inner profile mirrors outer profile at a constant wall offset.
featurePattern: Revolve combined trapezoid + rectangle profile (inlet taper + straight tip section), 360°.
failureModes: Throat (smallest diameter) going to zero collapses the geometry.
Inner and outer profiles must not cross.
validationRules: outletRadius > 0 for a viable flow path.
example_prompt: Nozzle 2 inch inlet 0.5 inch outlet 2 inch taper 1 inch straight tip

title: Gusset Or Diagonal Rib
summary: A gusset is a triangular stiffening plate added at the junction of two structural members. Sketch a right triangle profile and extrude to the member depth.
parameterHints: Expose gussetWidth (horizontal leg), gussetHeight (vertical leg), and gussetThickness.
Hypotenuse is the diagonal bracing face.
modelingNotes: Sketch a right triangle: (0,0), (width,0), (0,height) — three segments forming a closed triangle.
Extrude the triangle to gussetThickness.
Position at the junction of two parts using offset planes.
For an L-bracket gusset: place the right angle at the inner corner of the L.
Multiple gussets: pattern linearly along the length.
featurePattern: Right triangle sketch (3 line segments), skSolve, opExtrude to thickness.
failureModes: Open triangle — all 3 segments must connect.
Gusset positioned off-plane from the structure it reinforces.
example_prompt: Triangular gusset plate 2 inch base 1.5 inch height 0.1 inch thick

title: Multi-Body Composition Strategy
summary: Complex parts are built from multiple sub-bodies that are then unioned or subtracted. Build each sub-body as a separate opExtrude or opCylinder, then combine with opBoolean. This is the correct FS pattern for parts with multiple geometric sections.
parameterHints: Plan which bodies to create before writing code.
Label each sub-body with a descriptive suffix: id+'torso', id+'armL', id+'bore'.
Union adjacent bodies immediately after creating them.
modelingNotes: Pattern: create body A, create body B, opBoolean UNION B into A, create body C, opBoolean UNION C into (A+B).
For subtraction (holes, pockets): create tool body, opBoolean SUBTRACT tool from target.
qCreatedBy(id+'part1', EntityType.BODY) queries the body created by the operation named 'part1'.
The 'targets' body in UNION becomes the merged result — it absorbs 'tools'.
Never use the same id string for two operations — each opCylinder/opExtrude needs a unique id suffix.
featurePattern: opExtrude id+'main' → opCylinder id+'boss' → opBoolean UNION boss→main → opCylinder id+'bore' (full depth) → opBoolean SUBTRACT bore→main.
failureModes: Using duplicate id strings — second operation overwrites the first.
Subtracting before the bodies overlap — tool must intersect target.
Forgetting that 'tools' body is consumed by opBoolean — do not reference it after the boolean.
validationRules: Every op id string must be unique.
Tool body must geometrically intersect target body for SUBTRACTION.
example_prompt: Cylinder with a boss on top and a bore through the center

title: Offset Plane Construction
summary: To create geometry at different heights or on different faces, construct offset planes using the plane() function. This is essential for loft profiles, boss features, and any feature not on the main sketch plane.
parameterHints: Use definition.height or definition.depth values to position the offset plane.
For a plane at the top of an extruded body: offset = depth of the extrusion.
modelingNotes: Offset plane: var topPlane = plane(skPlane.origin + skPlane.normal * definition.height, skPlane.normal);
Perpendicular plane: var sidePlane = plane(skPlane.origin, skPlane.x);
Angled plane: use rotationAround() on the normal to create a tilted plane.
For loft: create planeA at origin, planeB at (origin + normal * height), sketch profiles on each.
For boss on top face: offsetPlane = plane(skPlane.origin + skPlane.normal * boxDepth, skPlane.normal).
plane() takes: plane(origin is Vector, normal is Vector) — both as 3D unit vectors.
featurePattern: var topPlane = plane(skPlane.origin + skPlane.normal * definition.height, skPlane.normal); var sk2 = newSketchOnPlane(context, id+'sk2', {'sketchPlane': topPlane});
failureModes: Using plane(skPlane.origin, skPlane.normal * definition.height) — wrong argument order.
Normal vector must be a unit vector — skPlane.normal is already unit length.
offset must use skPlane.normal multiplication, not skPlane.x.
validationRules: plane() takes (origin, normal) — not (point, vector, distance).
Normal of offset plane should match source plane normal for parallel planes.
example_prompt: Create a sketch plane 3 inches above the selected face

title: Sketch Constraint: skFitSpline For Organic Curves
summary: skFitSpline creates a smooth curve through a set of control points. Use for organic shapes, airfoils, cam profiles, and any continuously curved edge that cannot be described by arcs.
parameterHints: Use 4 to 7 control points for a smooth curve — 2 points gives a straight line.
Distribute control points proportionally — cluster near areas of high curvature.
Scale all points by inch: vector(x, y) * inch where x,y are unitless numbers.
modelingNotes: skFitSpline(sk, 'spline1', { 'points': [vector(x1,y1)*inch, vector(x2,y2)*inch, ...] });
The spline passes through all given points (interpolated spline, not Bezier control hull).
For a closed spline: make the last point equal to the first point.
For a smooth join: the spline end should align with connected line segments.
Do NOT use skFitSpline for circular arcs — use skArc instead.
4-point minimum for meaningful organic shape; 7-point maximum for simplicity.
featurePattern: skFitSpline with 4-7 control points, close with connecting line segments back to axis or starting point.
failureModes: 2-point spline = straight line — not organic.
Points not in sequence along the curve direction — spline will loop back on itself.
Spline not connected to adjacent segments — profile won't close.
validationRules: At least 3 control points (4+ recommended for organic).
End point of spline must connect to adjacent sketch entity.
example_prompt: Smooth organic curve with 5 control points

title: Sketch Arc With skArc
summary: skArc draws a circular arc through three points: start, a point on the arc (mid), and end. Use for rounded corners, dome profiles, pipe elbows, and any partial circular feature.
parameterHints: skArc needs start, mid (a point ON the arc), and end — not start, center, end.
For a quarter circle of radius R from (R,0) to (0,R): mid = vector(R*cos(45°), R*sin(45°)) ≈ vector(0.707R, 0.707R).
For a 90° arc: mid point is at 45° from center.
modelingNotes: skArc(sk, 'arc1', { 'start': vector(R,0)*inch, 'mid': vector(R*0.707, R*0.707)*inch, 'end': vector(0,R)*inch });
The mid point defines which side of the chord the arc bulges toward.
For a semicircle: start=(R,0), mid=(0,R) [90°], end=(-R,0) — but usually split into two quarter arcs.
Connect arc endpoints to adjacent sketch lines exactly — gaps prevent profile closure.
For a full circle: use skCircle, not skArc.
featurePattern: skArc with start, mid (at 45° from center for quarter arc), and end points, all in inch units.
failureModes: Mid point must be ON the arc, not at the center — center-based arc syntax doesn't exist in FS.
Mid point collinear with start and end — arc degenerates to a line.
Arc endpoints not aligned with adjacent line endpoints — open profile.
validationRules: mid must not be collinear with start and end.
All three points in the same sketch plane.
example_prompt: 90 degree arc from (1,0) to (0,1) inch

title: For Loop In Feature Body
summary: FeatureScript allows for loops inside the feature body to generate repeated geometry — bolt holes, gear teeth, fin arrays. Use const or var variables inside the loop.
parameterHints: Use isInteger(definition.count, {(unitless): [1, N, maxN]}) for loop count parameters.
Loop variable: for (var k = 0; k < definition.count; k += 1) { ... }
modelingNotes: For loop syntax in FS: for (var k = 0; k < N; k += 1) { ... }
++ and -- operators do NOT exist in FS — use k += 1.
Inside a loop, generate unique id strings: id + 'hole' ~ k
String concatenation uses ~, not + : 'hole' ~ k gives 'hole0', 'hole1', etc.
Sketch entity names in a loop: skCircle(sk, 'h' ~ k, { ... })
const inside a loop block: use var instead — const must be initialized in the same statement.
Loop-generated sketch entities: all in same sketch call → one skSolve → one opExtrude.
featurePattern: for (var k = 0; k < definition.count; k += 1) { var angle = 2 * PI * k / definition.count; skCircle(sk, 'hole' ~ k, { 'center': vector(R*cos(angle), R*sin(angle))*inch, 'radius': hR }); }
failureModes: Using k++ instead of k += 1 — ++ does not exist in FS.
Duplicate sketch entity names — each name must be unique; use ~ k suffix.
Using + for string concatenation — use ~ in FS.
Declaring const inside a loop when the value needs to change each iteration — use var.
validationRules: Each sketch entity in a loop must have a unique name string.
Loop increment must use k += 1, not k++.
example_prompt: 8 equally spaced holes around a circle

title: Lambda Functions Inside Feature Body
summary: Helper functions inside a feature body MUST be const lambda assignments, not named function declarations. Named top-level functions (function foo() {}) are illegal inside the feature lambda.
parameterHints: Define lambdas with const: const myFn = function(x) { return x * 2; };
Lambdas can close over surrounding variables (captures).
Arrow syntax also works: const double = (x) => x * 2;
modelingNotes: WRONG (inside feature body): function invPoint(t, rb) { return ...; }
CORRECT: const invPoint = function(t is number, rb is number) { return ...; };
Named top-level functions are allowed OUTSIDE the feature body at module level.
Lambdas can be passed to other functions and stored in variables.
For gear tooth math: define invPoint, rotPoint, mirrorPoint as const lambdas inside the feature.
Multiple lambdas can call each other if defined in the right order (invPoint before it's used).
featurePattern: const helperFn = function(arg is Type) { return result; }; — defined inside feature body before use.
failureModes: function foo() {} inside feature body — syntax error in FeatureScript.
Using a lambda before it's defined — FS is sequential, no hoisting.
Returning undefined from a lambda that should return a value.
validationRules: All helper functions inside feature body must use const lambda syntax.
Define lambdas before their first use.
example_prompt: Gear feature with involute tooth helper functions

title: isLength And isInteger Preconditions
summary: All feature parameters must be declared in the precondition block with isLength or isInteger. Never use 'definition.x is Length' — that is invalid FS syntax. Never multiply an isLength parameter by inch in the body.
parameterHints: Length: annotation { 'Name': 'Width', 'Default': '2 * inch' } isLength(definition.width, LENGTH_BOUNDS);
Zero-allowed length: isLength(definition.holeRadius, NONNEGATIVE_ZERO_INCLUSIVE_LENGTH_BOUNDS);
Integer: annotation { 'Name': 'Count', 'Default': '4' } isInteger(definition.count, {(unitless): [1, 4, 100]});
Boolean: annotation { 'Name': 'Add Fillet' } definition.addFillet is boolean;
modelingNotes: In the body, definition.width is already a Length value — never write definition.width * inch.
To get a pure number from a Length: var wNum = definition.width / inch; (then wNum is unitless).
For vector coordinates: vector(-definition.width/(2*inch), -definition.height/(2*inch)) * inch.
isLength with LENGTH_BOUNDS requires value > 0. Use NONNEGATIVE_ZERO_INCLUSIVE_LENGTH_BOUNDS for 0-allowed.
isInteger requires three bounds: {(unitless): [min, default, max]}.
featurePattern: annotation { 'Name': 'Width', 'Default': '2 * inch' } isLength(definition.width, LENGTH_BOUNDS); — in body: definition.width is already Length.
failureModes: definition.width is Length — invalid FS syntax (not a statement).
definition.width * inch — doubles the unit (definition.width is already Length, * inch = Length * Length).
isInteger(definition.count) — missing bounds map, fails in FS 2931.
definition.count >= 1; definition.count <= 100; — not valid in precondition for integers, use bounds map.
validationRules: All length parameters: isLength(definition.x, BOUNDS) — not 'is Length'.
example_prompt: Feature with width, height, hole count, and fillet radius parameters

title: Plane Selection Parameter
summary: Allow users to select which plane to sketch on by exposing a Query parameter with GeometryType.PLANE filter. In the body, resolve it with evPlane() and fall back to a default world plane.
parameterHints: Precondition: annotation { 'Name': 'Plane', 'Filter': GeometryType.PLANE, 'MaxNumberOfPicks': 1 } definition.location is Query;
Body: var skPlane = isQueryEmpty(context, definition.location) ? plane(WORLD_ORIGIN, Z_DIRECTION) : evPlane(context, { 'face': definition.location });
modelingNotes: isQueryEmpty returns true when the user has not selected any face/plane yet.
WORLD_ORIGIN and Z_DIRECTION are standard library constants for the top plane.
evPlane(context, { 'face': definition.location }) gets the plane of the selected face.
After getting skPlane: skPlane.origin is the plane center, skPlane.normal is the surface normal.
Always provide a fallback plane — never crash when no plane is selected.
For offset planes from the selected plane: plane(skPlane.origin + skPlane.normal * offset, skPlane.normal).
featurePattern: var skPlane = isQueryEmpty(context, definition.location) ? plane(WORLD_ORIGIN, Z_DIRECTION) : evPlane(context, { 'face': definition.location });
failureModes: Calling evPlane when no face is selected — throws error without isQueryEmpty guard.
Using definition.location directly as a plane — it's a Query, not a Plane.
Forgetting the fallback — feature fails when plane field is empty.
validationRules: Always guard evPlane with isQueryEmpty check.
definition.location is Query — must be declared with 'Filter': GeometryType.PLANE.
example_prompt: Feature that lets the user pick which face to sketch on

title: Encoder Or Sensor Mount Plate
summary: A rectangular plate with a central bore for a shaft and a bolt circle for mounting an encoder or sensor. Standard AMT103 bolt circle: 4x M3 holes on 25.8mm (1.016in) PCD, center bore 14mm (0.551in).
parameterHints: AMT103 mount: centerBore=0.551in radius (actually 14mm ID), boltCircle=0.508in radius (25.8mm PCD/2), 4 x 0.063in holes (M3 clearance).
NEO encoder: built-in — no separate mount needed.
CTRE CANCoder: 4x #10-32 holes on 1.5in bolt circle, 0.375in shaft bore.
modelingNotes: Pattern: rectangle plate + center bore circle + 4 bolt holes on PCD in one sketch.
For 4 holes at 90° intervals: x = boltR * cos(k * PI/2), y = boltR * sin(k * PI/2) for k=0,1,2,3.
qSketchRegion(id + 'sk', true) extrudes all regions with inner holes cut out.
Plate thickness 0.125 to 0.25 inch typical.
featurePattern: Rectangle + center circle + 4 bolt holes at 90° via for loop, qSketchRegion(true), opExtrude BLIND.
failureModes: Bolt holes overlapping center bore — check boltCircleRadius > boreRadius + holeRadius.
Plate too thin — less than 0.062 inch risks flex.
example_prompt: AMT103 encoder mount plate for 0.5 inch shaft

title: Motor Mounting Plate (CIM, NEO, Falcon 500)
summary: Motor face mounts are plates with the motor bolt pattern plus a central bore for the motor shaft. Each motor has a specific bolt pattern.
parameterHints: CIM/NEO/Falcon 500: same face plate — 4x 10-32 holes on 2in bolt circle (1in radius), center bore 0.874in radius (1.748in OD).
775pro: 2x 10-32 holes on 1.5in bolt circle opposite each other, 0.315in center bore.
BAG motor: 2x M3 holes on 1.5in bolt circle, 0.315in center bore.
Expose boltCircleRadius, boltHoleRadius, centerBoreRadius, plateThickness.
modelingNotes: Standard FRC motor face plate is typically circular (diameter matching motor face) or rectangular.
CIM/NEO/Falcon: 4 holes at 0°, 90°, 180°, 270° on 1in radius from center.
Center bore: 0.874in radius (snug motor register fit).
Add mounting holes for the gearbox or robot frame as additional hole pattern.
featurePattern: Circle plate (or rectangle) + center bore + 4 motor bolt holes at 90° intervals + additional mounting holes, qSketchRegion(true), opExtrude.
failureModes: Wrong bolt circle radius — double check against motor datasheet.
Center bore too large — motor register won't seat.
example_prompt: NEO motor mount plate 0.25 inch thick with standard 2 inch bolt circle

title: Slot Or Keyway Cut
summary: A slot or keyway is a rectangular cut into a shaft or bore. Use a rectangle sketch aligned to the shaft axis, extrude through the material, and subtract from the shaft body.
parameterHints: Standard keyways: 1/4 shaft = 1/16 key width, 3/8 shaft = 3/32 key, 1/2 shaft = 1/8 key.
Expose keyWidth, keyDepth (depth of cut into shaft), and keyLength.
keyDepth is typically half the key height.
modelingNotes: Method: sketch a rectangle on a plane passing through the shaft axis, extrude outward (past the shaft OD), subtract from shaft.
The cut rectangle: keyWidth wide, positioned at the shaft surface (y = shaftRadius - keyDepth).
Extend the extrude in both directions (symmetric) to ensure full material removal.
For a square key: keyWidth = keyHeight = shaftDiameter / 4.
opBoolean SUBTRACT the slot tool body from the shaft body.
featurePattern: Rectangle sketch on axial plane at shaft surface position, opExtrude beyond OD, opBoolean SUBTRACT from shaft.
failureModes: Slot plane not aligned with shaft axis — results in off-angle cut.
keyDepth > shaftRadius — cuts through the shaft center.
example_prompt: 1/8 inch keyway slot in 0.5 inch shaft 1.5 inches long

title: Snap Ring Or Retaining Ring Groove
summary: A snap ring groove is a shallow annular groove cut into a shaft or bore. Model as a thin subtracted torus or a revolve of a small rectangular notch profile.
parameterHints: Standard snap ring grooves: shaft diameter = D, groove diameter = D - 2*depth, groove width = ring thickness.
Expose shaftRadius, grooveDepth, and grooveWidth.
Typical groove depth = 0.04 to 0.08 inch.
modelingNotes: Method: revolve a small rectangle (grooveWidth x grooveDepth) at the groove position to create a ring-shaped cut.
The rectangle sits at (shaftR - grooveDepth, grooveY) in the profile plane.
Revolve 360° to create the tool body, then opBoolean SUBTRACT from shaft.
Profile: axis(0,0)→(0,shaftL), shaft side(shaftR, 0)→(shaftR, grooveY), notch rectangle, etc.
Simpler: sketch the full shaft profile with the groove notch included, revolve once — no boolean needed.
featurePattern: Shaft profile with small rectangular groove notch in the revolve profile, revolve 360° — one-operation approach.
failureModes: Groove too deep — approaches shaft center, weakens shaft.
Groove width too narrow — snap ring won't fit in tolerance.
example_prompt: 0.5 inch shaft with snap ring groove at 1 inch from end

title: Threaded Hole Pattern (Simplified)
summary: FeatureScript does not generate actual thread geometry — model threaded holes as simple cylindrical bores sized to the tap drill diameter. The thread is specified as a feature label parameter but not modeled geometrically.
parameterHints: M3 tap drill: 2.5mm (0.098in) radius = 0.049in. M4: 3.3mm rad=0.065in. M5: 4.2mm rad=0.083in. M6: 5mm rad=0.098in.
#10-32: 0.159in clearance, 0.120in tap radius. 1/4-20: 0.201in clearance, 0.161in tap radius.
Model as a simple bore circle — Onshape's Hole feature handles actual threads.
modelingNotes: For a FeatureScript custom feature, represent threaded holes as cylindrical bores at the tap drill size.
Place multiple threaded holes in a for loop: skCircle(sk, 'thread' ~ k, ...) with correct position.
The feature label or summary should note 'Thread not modeled — use Onshape Hole feature for actual threads'.
For FRC: M3 clearance hole (0.130in dia) is standard for structural bolts.
featurePattern: Circles at tap drill radius placed in sketch, qSketchRegion(true), opExtrude to material depth.
failureModes: Thread geometry is too complex for custom features — never attempt to generate helix threads.
Confusing clearance diameter with tap diameter — clearance holes are larger.
validationRules: Tap drill radius < clearance hole radius < head clearance radius.
M-thread tap drill ≈ (nominal diameter - pitch) in mm.
example_prompt: Four M4 threaded holes on a 1.5 inch bolt circle

title: Wing Or Airfoil Profile
summary: An airfoil cross-section is a teardrop-shaped closed curve. Approximate with a skFitSpline through a NACA 4-digit profile sample, or use a simpler lens shape for hobby applications.
parameterHints: Expose chord (length from leading to trailing edge), maxThickness, and wingspan/depth.
NACA 2412: max thickness 12% chord at 30% from leading edge.
modelingNotes: Sketch the upper and lower surfaces as two skFitSplines meeting at leading edge (0,0) and trailing edge (c,0).
Use 5-7 control points per surface for a smooth result.
The profile is in the YZ or XY plane; extrude along the third axis for wingspan.
For a swept wing: use opSweep with the airfoil as profile and a line/arc as span path.
For a tapered wing: use opLoft between root chord (full size) and tip chord (scaled).
featurePattern: Two skFitSplines (upper and lower surfaces) connecting at leading and trailing edges, skSolve, opExtrude to wingspan.
failureModes: Upper and lower splines not meeting at leading/trailing edge — open profile.
Too few control points — profile looks blocky.
Trailing edge too thick — add a sharp trailing point at (c,0).
validationRules: Both surfaces must meet at x=0 and x=chord.
example_prompt: NACA 2412 airfoil 4 inch chord 6 inch wingspan

title: Box Tube Or Square Tube
summary: A square or rectangular hollow tube is a box profile with a concentric inner cavity. Use two nested skRectangles in one sketch and extrude the ring region. Common for FRC and structural applications.
parameterHints: Expose outerWidth, outerHeight, wallThickness, and length.
Common FRC: 1x1x0.1, 2x1x0.1, 2x2x0.125 inch.
innerWidth = outerWidth - 2*wall, innerHeight = outerHeight - 2*wall.
modelingNotes: One sketch with two centered skRectangles: outer (full OD) and inner (OD minus 2*wall).
Outer: firstCorner=(-OW/2, -OH/2), secondCorner=(OW/2, OH/2) in inch-scaled form.
Inner: firstCorner=(-(OW/2-wall), -(OH/2-wall)), secondCorner=((OW/2-wall), (OH/2-wall)).
Use the inch-division pattern: vector(-definition.outerWidth/(2*inch), ...) * inch.
qSketchRegion(id+'sk', true) selects the ring region (outer minus inner).
opExtrude BLIND to definition.length.
featurePattern: Two nested centered rectangles (outer and inner), qSketchRegion(true), opExtrude to tube length.
failureModes: wall > outerWidth/2 or wall > outerHeight/2 — inner rectangle disappears, extrusion becomes solid.
Using vector(-0.5,-0.5)*definition.outerWidth — both components scale the same (wrong for non-square).
Must use: vector(-definition.outerWidth/(2*inch), -definition.outerHeight/(2*inch)) * inch.
example_prompt: 2x1 inch square tube 12 inches long 0.1 inch wall

title: Mounting Bracket With Slots
summary: A mounting plate with adjustment slots instead of fixed holes. Slots allow positional adjustment. Sketch slots as stadium shapes (rectangle + two semicircles) or as rectangular slots.
parameterHints: Expose slotLength, slotWidth (clearance hole size), numSlots, and slotSpacing.
Slot clearance: slotWidth ≈ bolt diameter + 0.01 inch.
For vertical slots: orient slot along the y-axis.
modelingNotes: Slot sketch: a rectangle (slotLength - slotWidth) x slotWidth plus two semicircles at the ends.
Or simpler: just skRectangle for a pure rectangular slot (no rounded ends) — still functional.
For rounded slots: use the stadium shape pattern (lines + arcs).
Place multiple slots in a for loop.
qSketchRegion(id, true) extrudes the plate with slot cutouts.
featurePattern: Plate rectangle + slot shapes (rectangle or stadium) in one sketch, qSketchRegion(true), opExtrude.
failureModes: Slots too close to edge — less than slotWidth/2 edge distance causes thin walls.
Slot width too small for the bolt — check clearance.
example_prompt: Mounting plate 4x2 inches with three vertical adjustment slots for 1/4 inch bolts

title: Compound Cylinder With Mounting Flange
summary: A cylinder body with an integrated base flange. Common for standoffs, bosses on plates, and motor output adapters. Build the cylinder first, then add the flange as a wider cylinder at the base.
parameterHints: Expose shaftRadius, flangeRadius, shaftHeight, flangeThickness.
flangeRadius > shaftRadius always.
Common standoff: shaftRadius = 0.25in, flangeRadius = 0.5in.
modelingNotes: Method 1: Sketch both circles at base, extrude to flangeThickness, then extrude the inner circle region additionally to shaftHeight.
Method 2: Revolve a stepped profile (wide at bottom for flange, narrow for shaft).
Revolve method is cleaner: profile has two widths (flangeR at y=0..flangeT, shaftR at y=flangeT..shaftH).
Add bolt holes: sketch 4 circles on the flange annulus and subtract.
featurePattern: Revolve stepped profile (flange width + shaft width) 360° for clean integrated result.
failureModes: Two separate extrudes without union — leaves two bodies.
Revolve profile must include the step geometry.
example_prompt: Flanged standoff 0.5 inch shaft 2 inches tall with 1 inch diameter base flange 0.25 inch thick

title: Differential Housing Or Gear Box Plate
summary: A gearbox plate is a rectangular or circular plate with precision bores for bearing/shaft locations. Each bore is at a specific center-to-center distance (C-C). Expose all bore positions as parameters.
parameterHints: For meshing gears: center distance = pitchRadius1 + pitchRadius2.
Expose inputBoreRadius, outputBoreRadius, centerDistance, and plate dimensions.
Typical FRC gearbox plate: 4x4 inch, 0.25 inch thick.
modelingNotes: Plate sketch: outer rectangle + input bore circle (at origin) + output bore circle (at centerDistance from origin).
Additional mounting holes around the perimeter.
Center distance is fixed by the gear pair — not adjustable.
Bore clearance for a bearing: bearingOD + 0 to -0.001 inch (light press).
Add lightening holes or pockets to reduce weight.
featurePattern: Rectangle + input bore at (0,0) + output bore at (C-C, 0) + mounting holes, qSketchRegion(true), opExtrude.
failureModes: Center distance wrong — gears won't mesh.
Bore too large — bearing won't press fit.
example_prompt: FRC gearbox plate for 8:1 reduction with 20DP gears

title: Knurled Or Textured Cylinder Approximation
summary: True knurl geometry is very complex. In FeatureScript, approximate a knurled surface as a plain cylinder with a note about knurl callout, or add shallow circumferential grooves using a for-loop of torus-slice subtractions.
parameterHints: Expose cylinderRadius, cylinderLength, and optionally grooveCount and grooveDepth.
Circumferential grooves: grooveSpacing = cylinderLength / grooveCount.
modelingNotes: Simple approach: generate a plain cylinder and note that knurling is a machining callout.
Groove approximation: subtract thin annular rings using a for loop of revolve-rectangle tools.
Each groove: revolve a small rectangle at (R - depth/2, grooveY) — creates a circumferential groove.
10-30 grooves is typical; more grooves slow regeneration significantly.
True diamond knurl would require 3D patterning beyond standard FS primitives.
featurePattern: Cylinder body + for loop of circumferential groove subtractions (revolve rectangle tool at each groove position).
failureModes: Too many grooves (>50) causes very slow regeneration.
Groove too deep — weakens the part.
example_prompt: Knurled grip cylinder 0.75 inch diameter 2 inches long with 20 grooves

title: Hook Or Cantilever Shape
summary: A hook is an extruded arc swept profile — a rectangular or circular cross-section following a C or J arc path. Use opSweep with an arc path and rectangular or circular profile.
parameterHints: Expose hookRadius (arc bend radius), hookAngle (arc sweep angle), profileWidth, profileHeight, and stemLength.
For a J-hook: 180° arc + straight stem. For a C-hook: 180° arc only.
modelingNotes: Path sketch: skArc for the curved section, connected to a skLineSegment for the straight stem.
Profile: skRectangle (rectangular cross-section) on a perpendicular plane.
Perpendicular plane for profile: plane(arcStartPoint, pathTangentAtStart).
opSweep: profiles = qSketchRegion(id+'prof'), path = qCreatedBy(id+'path', EntityType.EDGE).
For a circular rod hook: profile = skCircle.
featurePattern: Arc + line path sketch + perpendicular rectangular or circular profile sketch, opSweep.
failureModes: Profile plane not perpendicular to path tangent — produces twisted hook.
Path not fully connected — sweep fails on open/disconnected path.
example_prompt: J-hook 1 inch bend radius 0.25 inch square rod profile 3 inch stem

title: Rib Or Stiffening Wall
summary: Ribs are thin vertical walls added to strengthen flat plates or box walls. Sketch the rib profile directly (thin rectangle) and extrude, or use the rib profile at the junction of two faces.
parameterHints: Expose ribHeight, ribThickness, and ribLength.
Multiple parallel ribs: use a for loop with ribSpacing parameter.
Rib thickness is typically 0.5x to 1x the wall thickness it supports.
modelingNotes: Sketch a thin rectangle (ribLength x ribThickness) perpendicular to the main wall.
Extrude to ribHeight.
opBoolean UNION with the main body.
For multiple ribs: for loop of sketch placements at different y offsets.
Alternatively: extrude all ribs from a multi-rectangle sketch simultaneously.
featurePattern: Thin rectangle sketch for rib profile, opExtrude to ribHeight, opBoolean UNION into main body.
failureModes: Rib not unioned with main body — leaves separate floating wall.
ribThickness < 0.01 inch — too thin for most printing/machining.
example_prompt: Three parallel reinforcing ribs 0.1 inch thick 1 inch tall on a plate

title: Waffle Or Egg-Crate Structure
summary: A waffle structure is a grid of intersecting ribs forming pockets. Build as a solid block, subtract rectangular pockets in a grid pattern, or extrude the waffle profile from a sketch.
parameterHints: Expose gridSpacing, ribThickness, pocketDepth, gridCountX, and gridCountY.
pocketDepth = plateThickness - bottomWall.
Grid repeat: ribThickness + pocketWidth = gridSpacing.
modelingNotes: Method 1: Sketch both X and Y ribs as a series of rectangles in one sketch, extrude.
Method 2: Solid plate, then subtract a grid of rectangular pockets with a for loop.
For-loop double nested: for k_x in range: for k_y in range: create pocket at (kx*spacing, ky*spacing).
Pocket sketch: rectangle at each grid position, all in one sketch → one subtract.
Keep gridSpacing and ribThickness as parameters.
featurePattern: Double for-loop placing pocket rectangles in a grid sketch, qSketchRegion(true), opExtrude for pocket depth as subtract, or direct rib profile sketch.
failureModes: Pocket depth > plateThickness — cuts through the bottom.
Rib too thin to print or machine — keep > 0.04 inch.
example_prompt: 6x4 inch waffle plate 0.25 inch thick 0.5 inch grid 0.05 inch ribs

title: Involute Spline Or Hex Bore
summary: For hex bores (hex shaft interface): use skRegularPolygon with sides=6 as the inner cutout. For square bores: use a square skRectangle. Involute splines are too complex for custom features — use a simplified polygon approximation.
parameterHints: 1/2 inch hex shaft: across-flats = 0.5in, circumradius = 0.5/(sqrt(3)) = 0.2887in.
10mm hex: AF=10mm, circumradius = 10/sqrt(3) = 5.774mm = 0.227in.
For square bore: side = acrossFlats, circumradius = side * sqrt(2)/2.
modelingNotes: Hex bore: skRegularPolygon with sides=6 and firstVertex at circumradius, centered at (0,0).
The bore polygon is inside the outer shaft circle — use qSketchRegion(true) to subtract.
Square bore: two overlapping skRectangles rotated 45° — or use skRegularPolygon with sides=4 and 45° vertex.
For 1/2 inch hex bore: circumradius = 0.2887 inch; skRegularPolygon sides=6 firstVertex=(0.2887, 0)*inch.
featurePattern: Outer circle + inner skRegularPolygon (hex), qSketchRegion(true), opExtrude.
failureModes: acrossFlats ≠ circumradius — circumradius = AF / sqrt(3) for hex.
Polygon too large — removes all shaft material.
Using skPolygon — it does not exist in FS, use skRegularPolygon.
validationRules: sides = 6 for hex, sides = 4 for square bore.
example_prompt: Hub with 1/2 inch hex bore for FRC hex shaft

title: Chamfered Entry Hole Or Counterbore
summary: A counterbore is a stepped hole: wide bore at the top for screw head, narrow bore through the bottom for the shank. Build with a concentric two-circle sketch and extrude at two depths, or use boolean subtract in two passes.
parameterHints: Socket head cap screws (metric): M3 head OD=5.5mm, head height=3mm. M4: OD=7mm H=4mm. M5: OD=8.5mm H=5mm.
Socket head cap screws (imperial): 1/4-20 head OD=0.375in, head height=0.25in.
Expose clearanceBoreRadius, cboreRadius, cboreDepth, and throughBoreRadius.
modelingNotes: Sketch 1 on top face: large circle (cboreRadius), extrude DOWN cboreDepth.
Sketch 2 at bottom of cbore: small circle (clearanceBoreRadius), extrude DOWN remaining thickness.
Or: one sketch with two concentric circles, two separate extrude depth calls.
For countersink: revolve a V-notch profile or use the concentric sketch with 90° chamfer geometry.
opBoolean SUBTRACT both from the main body.
featurePattern: Two separate bore circles + two-depth extrude subtract ops — cbore at top depth, clearance bore through bottom.
failureModes: cboreRadius < clearanceBoreRadius — invalid, head bore must be larger.
cboreDepth >= plateThickness — countersinks through the entire plate.
example_prompt: Counterbore for M4 socket head cap screw in 0.5 inch plate
